blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Emergency Provisions are contained in Part XVIII (Articles 352–360) and were primarily inspired by the Weimar Constitution of Germany.
During an emergency, India's normal federal system transforms into a unitary structure, granting paramount powers to the Central Government.
National Emergency (Article 352) requires written advice from the Cabinet and a special majority parliamentary approval within 1 month.
The 44th Constitutional Amendment (1978) substituted 'Internal Disturbance' with 'Armed Rebellion' and made Articles 20 and 21 non-suspendable.
President's Rule (Article 356) can be imposed for failure of constitutional machinery in a state and is subject to judicial review following the landmark S.R. Bommai Case (1994).
Financial Emergency (Article 360) allows reduction of government salaries and central control over state finances, but has never been declared in India.
INTRODUCTION

blocks.content: The Emergency Provisions of the Indian Constitution are one of the most powerful and sensitive parts of the Constitution.They enable the Central Government to deal with extraordinary situations that threaten the security, stability, unity, or financial integrity of the nation.These provisions are contained in Part XVIII (Articles 352–360) of the Constitution.During an Emergency, the normal federal structure of India changes into a unitary form, giving maximum powers to the Centre to deal with the crisis.
The framers of the Constitution included emergency provisions to:

items:
• Protect sovereignty and territorial integrity
  • Deal with war, aggression, rebellion, or financial crisis
  • Maintain constitutional governance
  • Ensure unity and integrity of India
  • Prevent breakdown of administration

blocks.content: These provisions were inspired mainly by the Weimar Constitution of Germany.
The Indian Constitution provides for three types of emergencies:

items: National Emergency – Article 352
State Emergency (President’s Rule) – Article 356
Financial Emergency – Article 360

blocks.content: A National Emergency can be proclaimed when the security of India or any part of it is threatened due to:

items:
• War
  • External Aggression
  • Armed Rebellion

44th Amendment Safeguards: Replaced 'Internal Disturbance' with 'Armed Rebellion', made written advice of the Union Cabinet mandatory for Article 352, and prohibited the suspension of Fundamental Rights under Articles 20 and 21.
Judicial Review: Following the landmark S.R. Bommai Case (1994), President's Rule under Article 356 is subject to judicial scrutiny, preventing arbitrary imposition.

Extension Limit: President's Rule can be extended beyond 1 year (up to a maximum of 3 years) only if a National Emergency is in force OR the Election Commission certifies that assembly elections cannot be held.
Zero Occurrence: Financial Emergency under Article 360 is the only type of emergency that has never been imposed in India till date.

blocks.content: Emergency provisions must be used carefully.
They are meant to protect democracy, not destroy it. Hence, constitutional safeguards are very important.
The Emergency provisions of the Indian Constitution are essential for protecting the nation during extraordinary situations.
However, their misuse can threaten democracy.
The 44th Amendment has played a crucial role in restoring balance between authority and liberty.
